newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN seeks home for 260 boatpeople now in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: UN seeks home for 260 boatpeople now in Hong Kong.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency said on Tuesday it would press countries offering asylum to take in 260 of "the most deserving and viable cases" of Vietnamese boatpeople still in Hong Kong before the territory reverts to Chinese rule on July 1.

They are among 1,300 Vietnamese refugees registered at Pillar Point open refugee camp, along with 2,000 non-refugees considered to be economic migrants, Pamela O'Toole, spokeswoman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), told a news briefing.
But the 260 -- most of whom have been rejected by more than one resettlement country -- may be hard to place as they are among the last and some have minor criminal records, she said.
UNHCR will host a meeting in Geneva on May 26 on Hong Kong's boatpeople, remnants of 214,000 who fled Vietnam for the British colony following the 1975 communist victory in the Vietnam War.

Hong Kong, plagued by sporadic violence and riots by failed asylum-seekers in its detention centres since it began forced evictions in late 1991, has been trying to clear its camps before its final handover to China.
"We'll be asking donor governments to reconsider one last time some 260 of the most deserving and viable cases among them for resettlement," O'Toole said.
"Most of these people have already been put forward for resettlement once or even twice but have been rejected by one or more resettlement countries," she added.
About 140,000 of the 214,000 Vietnamese boatpeople who went to Hong Kong since 1975 have been resettled, according to UNHCR. Some 65,000 have been returned, 55,000 of them voluntarily.

"We would obviously like to see it cleared up before the final handover. If you ask me frankly, it might be difficult to get all of those refugees out of there, but we'll try our best," the spokeswoman said.
The last members of a refugee caseload are always the most difficult to place for various reasons, according to O'Toole.
"There might be some people with criminal records among them," she said of the group of 260.

"The group we put forward are not people who have serious criminal records -- they are not murderers or drug peddlers or anything that governments might be particularly concerned about," the spokeswoman added. "It is small-scale stuff."

UNHCR hoped that non-refugees -- those screened and found to be economic migrants rather than deserving international protection under the 1951 U.N. refugee convention -- would return to their homeland voluntarily.

"We hope that by May 31st -- which is one month before the handover and the date at which Vietnam says it will stop screening and clearing these people for return -- we will have less than 1,000 non-refugees," O'Toole said.
"We expect most of these 2,000 non-refugees we have at the moment to return voluntarily (to Vietnam)," she added.

Vietnamese boatpeople also fled in waves to Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand. The last camp, at Siqhui, Thailand, closed in February. There are 1,650 Vietnamese non-refugees in the Philippines, which has said it will let them remain pending repatriation or other solutions.
In all, some 755,300 Vietnamese have been resettled in third countries, with the highest number taken by the United States, according to UNHCR figures.
